content: Azithromycin is an oral macrolide antibacterial agent approved by the FDA for treating sexually transmitted diseases, mycobacterial infections, community-acquired pneumonia, and pelvic inflammatory disease. Common side effects include diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain, and vomiting. For adults, the recommended dosage varies by condition: For non-gonococcal urethritis and cervicitis caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, a single 1-gram dose is recommended. To prevent disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) infections, 1200 mg is taken once weekly, often combined with rifabutin. For treating disseminated MAC infections, 600 mg daily is combined with ethambutol (15 mg/kg daily). Additional antimycobacterial drugs may be added at the physician's discretion. For community-acquired pneumonia, 500 mg is administered intravenously daily for at least two days, followed by 500 mg orally daily to complete a 7-10 day course. For pelvic inflammatory disease, 500 mg is given intravenously daily for 1-2 days, followed by 250 mg orally daily to complete a 7-day course. If anaerobic microorganisms are suspected, an additional antimicrobial agent with anaerobic activity should be used. Off-label adult uses include: Azithromycin 500 mg orally daily for at least three months (supported by CDC/NIH/IDSA guidelines). A single 1-gram oral dose for certain infections (CDC-supported). Other regimens include 500 mg initially, followed by 250 mg daily for seven days, or 1 gram on day one followed by 500 mg daily for six days. For pediatric patients: Limited FDA-labeled indications exist, but off-label uses include 15 mg/kg orally for certain conditions. A single dose of 20 mg/kg (up to 1 gram) is also used off-label. Contraindications include hypersensitivity to azithromycin, erythromycin, or other macrolides/ketolides, and a history of cholestatic jaundice or hepatic dysfunction associated with prior azithromycin use. Warnings and precautions: Serious allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis and Stevens-Johnson syndrome, have been reported. Allergic symptoms may recur after discontinuation of symptomatic therapy. Hepatotoxicity, including liver failure and death, has been reported. Discontinue azithromycin immediately if signs of hepatitis occur. QT prolongation and torsades de pointes have been observed, particularly in at-risk populations (e.g., those with congenital long QT syndrome, bradyarrhythmias, or uncorrected hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia). Elderly patients may be more susceptible. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported and may range from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. CDAD should be considered in patients presenting with diarrhea after antibiotic use. Exacerbation of myasthenia gravis symptoms has been reported. Adverse reactions: Most adverse reactions are mild to moderate and reversible upon discontinuation. Common gastrointestinal reactions include diarrhea, nausea, and abdominal pain. Serious reactions include angioedema, cholestatic jaundice, and hearing impairment (especially at higher doses). Postmarketing reports include arrhythmias, QT prolongation, torsades de pointes, and various gastrointestinal, hepatic, and dermatologic reactions. Drug interactions: Co-administration with nelfinavir increases azithromycin serum concentrations, warranting close monitoring for adverse effects. Azithromycin may potentiate the effects of oral anticoagulants like warfarin, necessitating careful monitoring of prothrombin times. Potential interactions with digoxin and phenytoin require careful patient monitoring. Use in specific populations: Pregnancy: Classified as Category B by the FDA. Animal studies show no fetal harm, but human studies are lacking. Use only if clearly needed. Nursing mothers: Azithromycin is excreted in breast milk in small amounts; caution is advised. Pediatric use: Safety and efficacy for preventing or treating MAC in HIV-infected children have not been established. Geriatric use: No significant differences in safety or efficacy were observed compared to younger patients, but older individuals may be more sensitive to QT prolongation and torsades de pointes. Pharmacology: Azithromycin binds to the 50S ribosomal subunit of susceptible microorganisms, inhibiting protein synthesis without affecting nucleic acid synthesis. It concentrates in phagocytes and fibroblasts, potentially aiding drug distribution to inflamed tissues. Azithromycin is available as tablets and oral suspension, containing azithromycin dihydrate as the active ingredient, along with various inactive ingredients.
